overview.title: Building a frequency-limited vocabulary and a word-level tokenizer
overview.main_topic: Finishing CharTokenizer, computing a character vocabulary capped at the max_size most frequent tokens (Listing 14.2), and defining WordTokenizer by swapping in the word regex (Listing 14.3)
overview.central_idea: A tokenizer needs a vocabulary learned from data. Listing 14.2 counts tokens with collections.Counter, reserves index 0 for [UNK], keeps only the most common max_size - 1 tokens, and returns a token -> index dict. Limiting vocabulary size matters because it limits the number of model parameters. A word-level tokenizer is the same class with a different split regex.
overview.importance: Building a vocabulary from frequency counts with a size cap is the standard way vocabularies are made (Keras' TextVectorization and later subword tokenizers do the same thing at larger scale). The max_size knob directly controls embedding and output-layer sizes in later models.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 14.2 line by line: Counter, most_common, [UNK] at index 0, enumerate to dict
Explain why the cap is max_size - len(vocabulary)
Explain why limiting vocabulary size limits model parameters
Identify the one difference between WordTokenizer and CharTokenizer

paragraphs.excerpt: Pretty simple. Before using this, we also need to build a function
paragraphs.what_it_says: The tokenizer is simple, but before using it we need a function that computes a vocabulary from input text. Rather than mapping all characters to unique indices, the function can limit the vocabulary to the most common tokens. Once modelling starts, limiting vocabulary size will be an important way to limit the number of parameters in a model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The vocabulary is learned from a corpus, much like model weights are learned from data. Capping it at max_size keeps the frequent tokens (where the data is) and sends rare ones to [UNK]. Model components whose size scales with the vocabulary, such as one-hot input width, embedding tables (V x d) and softmax output layers (d x V), shrink accordingly.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The vocabulary size is a real hyperparameter. Later the chapter's bag-of-words and embedding models are sized by it, and p.414 shows the tension: word vocabularies fill up quickly, and tight caps push much text to [UNK].
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: an Embedding layer with vocabulary V and dimension d has V*d parameters; for V = 20,000 and d = 256 that is 5.12 million parameters, so halving V halves this layer.

terminology.meaning: The maximum number of entries, including [UNK], kept in the vocabulary.
Tokens with the highest counts in the training corpus.

connections: p.411: Listing 14.1 takes a vocabulary as a constructor argument.
p.414: a word vocabulary quickly fills 2,000 terms; the full book needs about 17,000.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The same approach works for a word-level tokenizer: reuse the character tokenizer's code with a different splitting step.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because the pipeline is factored into standardize/split/index, changing the token granularity means changing only the split rule (and then building a vocabulary with the matching rule, Listing 14.4 on p.413).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that the tokenizer design is modular. Subword tokenizers (14.2.2) also change mainly the splitting step and the vocabulary-building procedure.

concepts.name: Frequency-limited vocabulary
concepts.definition: A vocabulary built by counting tokens in the training data and keeping only the max_size most common (including [UNK]).
concepts.intuition: Give your few available ticket numbers to the tokens you will meet most often.
concepts.technical: Counter over tokens -> most_common(k) sorted by count -> list ["[UNK]", t1, ..., tk] -> dict token -> position. Index order equals frequency rank.
concepts.significance: Controls the size of parameter matrices tied to the vocabulary; rare tokens fall back to [UNK].
concepts.example: With max_size=4 on "aab c": counts a:2, b:1, ' ':1, c:1 -> vocabulary {[UNK]:0, a:1, b:2, ' ':3} (ties broken by first appearance).
concepts.misconception: max_size counts [UNK] too; only max_size - 1 real tokens are kept.

concepts.name: Vocabulary size and parameter count
concepts.definition: The book notes that limiting vocabulary size is an important way to limit the number of parameters in a model.
concepts.intuition: Each vocabulary entry needs its own row of weights somewhere in the model.
concepts.technical: Not in the book on this page: for one-hot/multi-hot input into a Dense layer with u units, parameters = V*u + u; an Embedding layer has V*d; a softmax output over the vocabulary has d*V + V.
concepts.significance: Vocabulary size becomes one of the main levers on model size in chapters 14-15.
concepts.example: Dense(16) on a 20,000-dim multi-hot input: 20,000*16 + 16 = 320,016 parameters.
concepts.misconception: A bigger vocabulary is not free: it increases parameters and needs more data per token.

concepts.name: Modular tokenizer design
concepts.definition: A tokenizer class whose standardize, split and index steps are separate methods, so variants differ in one method.
concepts.intuition: Swap the blade, keep the machine.
concepts.technical: WordTokenizer = CharTokenizer with split() using r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" instead of r".".
concepts.misconception: The vocabulary must be built with the same split rule as the tokenizer, otherwise lookups miss.

code.title: End of Listing 14.1 (CharTokenizer.__call__)
code.what_it_does: Completes __call__ from p.411: index the tokens and return the list of integers. The rest of the class is on p.411.

line_explanations.explanation: Maps each character token to its vocabulary index, with unk_id for unknown characters.
Returns the list of ints, one per character of the lowercased input (newlines excluded by the "." regex).

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the token list from split(). Output: list of int indices.
code.algorithm: Last stage of standardize -> split -> index.
pitfalls: Returns a Python list, not a tensor; batching and padding into tensors come later.

code.title: Computing a character-level vocabulary
code.what_it_does: Counts characters over an iterable of strings and returns a dict from the top max_size - 1 characters (plus [UNK]) to indices ordered by frequency.

line_explanations.explanation: Defines the function; char_counts is a dict-like counter of token frequencies.
For each input string (e.g. one line of a book): lowercase it (same standardization as CharTokenizer), split it into characters (same split), and add the counts.
Starts the vocabulary with [UNK] so it gets index 0.
most_common(k) returns the k most frequent (token, count) pairs in descending order; k = max_size - 1 leaves room for [UNK].
Appends the tokens (counts are discarded) in frequency order.
Builds the token -> index dict from list positions: [UNK] -> 0, most frequent -> 1, ...

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: an iterable of strings and an int max_size. Output: dict of at most max_size entries. On Moby Dick with max_size=100 it returns 64 entries (p.413), because only 63 distinct lowercase characters occur.
code.algorithm: Frequency counting followed by top-k selection.
code.theory_link: The vocabulary from p.409, now learned from data and size-limited to control model parameters.

parameters.name: inputs
parameters.role: Iterable of training strings (e.g. lines of a text file).

parameters.name: max_size
parameters.role: Upper bound on vocabulary entries, [UNK] included.

pitfalls: If the corpus has fewer distinct tokens than max_size - 1, the vocabulary is simply smaller (64 < 100 on p.413).
Standardization and splitting are duplicated from CharTokenizer; if one changes and the other doesn't, lookups silently miss and return [UNK].
Ties in counts are ordered by first insertion (Counter.most_common behaviour), so ordering among equally frequent tokens depends on the data order.
Newlines are never counted because "." does not match "\n".
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written illustration (not from the book)
lines = ["The cat", "the hat"]
v = compute_char_vocabulary(lines, max_size=5)
print(v)
# counts: t:4, h:3, e:2, ' ':2, a:2, c:1 -> keep top 4
# {'[UNK]': 0, 't': 1, 'h': 2, 'e': 3, ' ': 4}

code.what_it_does: Defines a word-level tokenizer, identical to CharTokenizer except for the split regex. The final two lines of __call__ (indices = self.index(tokens); return indices) are on p.413.

line_explanations.explanation: Same constructor: store the vocabulary and the [UNK] id.
The only change: split into runs of word characters or single punctuation marks from [.,!?;].
Same indexing with the unk_id fallback.

code.inputs_outputs: Construct with a word vocabulary containing [UNK]; calling it on a string returns word indices.
code.theory_link: Word-level tokenization: shorter sequences, larger vocabulary.

parameters.name: vocabulary
parameters.role: Word -> index dict, built by compute_word_vocabulary (Listing 14.4, p.413).

pitfalls: Apostrophes and other punctuation not in [.,!?;] are dropped ("isn't" -> "isn", "t").
Beyond the book: the duplication between the two classes could be removed by subclassing and overriding split; the book keeps them separate for clarity.

deeper.title: Why max_size - len(vocabulary)?
deeper.body: At that line `vocabulary = ["[UNK]"]`, so `len(vocabulary)` is 1 and the call is `most_common(max_size - 1)`. After appending, the list has 1 + (max_size - 1) = max_size entries (or fewer if the corpus has fewer distinct tokens). Writing `len(vocabulary)` instead of 1 means the formula stays right if more special tokens (e.g. a padding token) are added to the initial list.

deeper.title: Vocabulary size and parameters: numbers
deeper.body:
Suppose a model embeds each token in d = 128 dimensions.

| tokenizer | V | embedding parameters V*d |
|---|---|---|
| characters (Moby Dick, p.413) | 64 | 8,192 |
| words capped at 2,000 (p.414) | 2,000 | 256,000 |
| all words in the book (~17,000, p.414) | 17,000 | 2,176,000 |

This is why the authors say limiting vocabulary size is an important way to limit parameters. (Table computed for these notes; V values are from pp.413-414.)

deeper.title: Zipf's law makes the cap cheap
deeper.body: Beyond the book: token frequencies in natural language roughly follow Zipf's law, so a small number of types accounts for most occurrences. Keeping the most common tokens therefore covers most of the running text, while the long tail of rare words that maps to [UNK] is a small fraction of tokens, though not of distinct words. Subword tokenization (p.414) attacks that tail differently.

misconceptions.correction: Only the split regex differs; standardize, index and __call__ are identical.

misconceptions.claim: Vocabulary size only affects preprocessing speed.
misconceptions.correction: The book stresses it is an important way to limit the number of parameters in a model.

takeaways: CharTokenizer.__call__ ends by indexing the tokens and returning the list of ints.
A vocabulary is computed from data by counting tokens and keeping the most common ones.
[UNK] is placed first (index 0); max_size includes it.
Indices are assigned in descending frequency order via enumerate.
Limiting vocabulary size is an important way to limit model parameters.
WordTokenizer differs from CharTokenizer only in its split regex.

questions.question: With max_size=100, at most how many distinct characters (excluding [UNK]) does compute_char_vocabulary keep?
questions.explanation: most_common(max_size - len(vocabulary)) with len(vocabulary) = 1 keeps 99 tokens, plus [UNK] = 100 entries. 64 is what Moby Dick actually yields on p.413 (63 characters + [UNK]), because the book has fewer distinct characters than the cap.

questions.question: Which index does the most frequent character get, and why?
questions.answer: Index 1, because [UNK] occupies index 0 and tokens are appended in descending frequency order before enumerate assigns positions.
questions.explanation: vocabulary starts as ["[UNK]"], then most_common's ordered tokens are appended.

questions.question: Why do the authors want to limit vocabulary size?
questions.answer: Because, on the modelling side, limiting vocabulary size is an important way to limit the number of parameters in a model; rare tokens can go to [UNK].
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph before Listing 14.2. Layers such as embeddings have one parameter row per vocabulary entry.

questions.question: What is the only difference between Listing 14.1 and Listing 14.3?
questions.explanation: WordTokenizer uses r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" instead of r".". Both lowercase, both use unk_id, and both return lists of ints.

questions.question: Why does compute_char_vocabulary lowercase and split exactly like CharTokenizer does?
questions.answer: The vocabulary must contain the same token strings the tokenizer will produce; otherwise lookups would miss and many tokens would map to [UNK] (e.g. uppercase letters never present in the vocabulary).
questions.explanation: Consistency between vocabulary building and tokenization is required for correct indexing.

questions.question: An embedding layer has V*d parameters. If you cap a word vocabulary at 2,000 instead of the about 17,000 words needed for all of Moby Dick (p.414), with d = 64, how many parameters do you save?
questions.explanation: Parameters scale linearly with V: 17,000*64 = 1,088,000 vs. 2,000*64 = 128,000. This illustrates the page's point that vocabulary size limits parameter count (the embedding formula is not on this page).

questions.question: Trace compute_char_vocabulary(["aba"], max_size=3) by hand. What dict comes out?
questions.explanation: Counts: a:2, b:1; most_common(2) gives [(a,2),(b,1)]; with [UNK] first, enumerate gives 0, 1, 2.
